summary: Shows how the AES Galois Counter Mode can provide both confidentiality and data integrity in the SSH transport layer. It is informational.

eli5.summary: SSH locks your messages. This describes one lock that also checks nobody changed what is inside.

questions: how does gcm work in ssh
subtitle: Using a single cipher to provide both encryption and integrity checking in secure remote login

tldr.problem: SSH traditionally uses two separate algorithms: one to encrypt data (keeping it secret) and another to authenticate it (proving it was not modified). Using two algorithms is less efficient than using one that does both.
tldr.mechanism: AES Galois Counter Mode is an encryption algorithm that produces both a ciphertext and an authentication tag in one operation, providing both confidentiality and data integrity. The document shows how to integrate AES-GCM into SSH's transport layer to replace the separate encryption and MAC algorithms.
tldr.outcome: SSH implementations can now optionally use AES-GCM for better performance, especially in hardware, while maintaining the same security properties and SSH message formats.

today: RFC 5647 is an Informational document published in August 2009. AES-GCM for SSH is now widely supported in modern SSH implementations, including OpenSSH, as it provides performance benefits especially in hardware-accelerated environments. The IANA registries for SSH encryption and MAC algorithms include the AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM entries as specified in this document.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Secure Shell (SSH) is the standard secure remote-login protocol for the Internet. SSH provides authentication, confidentiality and data integrity. Traditionally, SSH achieves confidentiality by encrypting data with an algorithm like AES, and achieves integrity by computing a message authentication code (MAC) with a separate algorithm. Galois Counter Mode (GCM) is a block cipher mode of operation that provides both confidentiality and data integrity in a single operation. AES-GCM is particularly well suited for efficient implementation, both in software and especially in hardware, because it uses counter mode for encryption (which can be pipelined) and uses arithmetic operations in the Galois Field for authentication (which can be efficiently implemented). This document specifies how to integrate AES-GCM into the SSH Transport Layer Protocol as an alternative to the traditional two-algorithm approach.
sections.eli5: SSH usually locks your messages with encryption and checks them with a separate stamp. GCM does both jobs in one operation, which is faster to compute and implement.

sections.title: How Galois Counter Mode Works
sections.content:
Galois Counter Mode is a mode of operation for block ciphers that combines encryption and authentication. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published the official specification. AES-GCM uses AES as the underlying block cipher and produces three key outputs: a ciphertext (the encrypted plaintext), an authentication tag (a cryptographic check value), and uses an initialization vector (IV, also called a nonce) to ensure that the same key is never used twice with the same IV.

GCM performs authenticated encryption by taking a plaintext, some additional authenticated data (data that is authenticated but not encrypted), an initialization vector and an encryption key. It outputs ciphertext and an authentication tag. For decryption, it takes ciphertext, additional authenticated data, the authentication tag, the initialization vector and the key, and outputs either the plaintext (if the tag is valid) or a failure indicator. Critically, GCM must validate the authentication tag before returning any plaintext, ensuring that a receiver never returns unverified data to the application.
sections.eli5: GCM takes your message, secret key and a random number, and outputs a scrambled message and a check tag. To unscramble, it checks the tag first, and only if it's good does it give you the message back.

sections.title: Secure Shell Protocol
sections.content:
SSH establishes secure tunnels between a client and server. The key exchange protocol (defined in RFC 4253) negotiates a shared secret and produces symmetric encryption keys. SSH encrypts all traffic after the initial key exchange using binary packets, each containing a packet length field, padding length, payload data, random padding, and a message authentication code.

During key exchange, both sides agree on encryption and MAC algorithms. For each direction (client-to-server and server-to-client), the key derivation function produces an initial IV, an encryption key, and an integrity key. When a new encryption algorithm is negotiated, a new set of symmetric keys is derived. The sequence number (which counts the number of packets sent) is used in the MAC calculation to protect against reordering attacks.
sections.eli5: SSH talks between two computers using a series of encrypted packets. Each packet has data, padding, and a check code. The two computers first agree on which encryption method to use, then derive keys from a shared secret.

sections.title: AES-GCM in SSH
sections.content:
SSH can use two AES-GCM variants: AEAD_AES_128_GCM (with a 128-bit key) and AEAD_AES_256_GCM (with a 256-bit key). Both produce a 16-octet authentication tag. Because AES-GCM combines encryption and authentication, the separate integrity key used by traditional SSH algorithms is not needed.

The initialization vector (IV) for AES-GCM is 12 octets, split into a 4-octet fixed field (derived during key exchange) and an 8-octet invocation counter field that increments after each packet. AES-GCM internally generates keystream blocks by encrypting a structure containing the fixed field, invocation counter and a block counter, producing 16 octets of keystream per block, which is then XORed with the plaintext to encrypt it.

When using AES-GCM in SSH, the plaintext passed to the encryption function consists of the padding length, payload and random padding (all of which must be encrypted). The additional authenticated data is the 4-octet packet length field. The encrypted binary packet is then constructed as the 4-octet packet length (in plaintext), the ciphertext, and the 16-octet authentication tag.
sections.eli5: SSH can use AES-GCM in two sizes: 128-bit keys or 256-bit keys, both producing a 16-byte check tag. The encryption counter starts fresh for each packet, and the packet length is authenticated but not encrypted.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: One potential concern is that SSH traditionally requires encryption of the entire binary packet, including the packet length field. However, GCM requires that plaintext not be returned until the authentication tag is verified, creating a problem: to parse a packet and find the authentication tag, you need to know the packet length; but you cannot decrypt the packet length until you have verified the tag. SSH AES-GCM solves this by treating the packet length as additional authenticated data (authenticated but not encrypted), rather than encrypting it as SSH normally requires. This is a deviation from the standard, but acceptable because: (1) encryption of the packet length does not significantly hide the packet length in practice, since bursts of packets reveal lengths through timing; (2) SSH provides random padding and SSH_MSG_IGNORE messages which are more effective at obscuring packet structure; and (3) the sequence number is involved in the authentication tag through the invocation counter, providing the security properties SSH requires.
sections.eli5: Usually SSH encrypts everything including the packet size. GCM doesn't let you check the message until you know its size, so we authenticate the size without encrypting it. This still works because padding and fake messages can hide the real size anyway.

data.title: Packet layout
data.code:
uint32   packet_length;     // Packet length (not encrypted)
byte     ciphertext[...];   // Encrypted padding_length, payload, padding
byte     auth_tag[16];      // 16-octet authentication tag
